text: Parks and Recreation (also known as Parks and Rec) is an American political satire mockumentary television sitcom created by Greg Daniels and Michael Schur. The series aired on NBC from April 9, 2009, to February 24, 2015, for 125 episodes across seven seasons, with a special reunion episode airing on April 30, 2020. It stars Amy Poehler as Leslie Knope, a perky, mid-level bureaucrat in the Parks and Recreation Department of the fictional town of Pawnee, Indiana. The ensemble cast includes Rashida Jones as Ann Perkins, Aziz Ansari as Tom Haverford, Nick Offerman as Ron Swanson, Aubrey Plaza as April Ludgate, Chris Pratt as Andy Dwyer, Paul Schneider as Mark Brendanawicz, Adam Scott as Ben Wyatt, Rob Lowe as Chris Traeger, Jim O'Heir as Garry "Jerry" Gergich, Retta as Donna Meagle, and Billy Eichner as Craig Middlebrooks. The writers researched local California politics and consulted with urban planners and elected officials. Leslie Knope underwent significant changes after the first season due to audience feedback that she seemed unintelligent and "ditzy." The show incorporated current events, such as a government shutdown in Pawnee inspired by the 2008 financial crisis. Real-life political figures, including John McCain, Michelle Obama, Newt Gingrich, and Joe Biden, made cameos in later episodes. The series was part of NBC's "Comedy Night Done Right" programming during its Thursday night prime-time block. It received mixed reviews in its first season, including comparisons to The Office, a sitcom also produced by Daniels and Schur, but after a re-approach to its tone and format, the second and subsequent seasons were widely acclaimed. Parks and Recreation earned 14 Primetime Emmy Award nominations (two for Outstanding Comedy Series), a Golden Globe Award win for Poehler's performance, a Golden Globe nomination for Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy, and a Peabody Award. In Time's 2012 year-end list, it was named the number one television series of that year. In 2013, after four consecutive nominations, it won the Television Critics Association Award for Outstanding Achievement in Comedy. The first season centers on Leslie Knope, deputy director of the Parks and Recreation Department in Pawnee, Indiana, as she promises to turn a construction pit beside Ann Perkins' house into a park after her boyfriend Andy Dwyer falls into it and breaks both legs, despite resistance from parks director Ron Swanson, an anti-government libertarian. City planner Mark Brendanawicz, whom Leslie has romantic feelings for, pragmatically argues the project is unrealistic due to government red tape but secretly convinces Ron to approve it. Leslie and her staff, including assistant Tom Haverford and intern April Ludgate, attempt to encourage community interest but face resistance. In the second season, the pit is eventually filled in when Leslie fills it in without permission, not realizing Andy was in it; Andy becomes injured and works with Leslie to threaten to sue the city unless the pit is filled. Mark leaves his city hall job for a private sector position. A crippling budget deficit leads state auditors Chris Traeger and Ben Wyatt to temporarily shut down the Pawnee government. The third season opens with the government reopened but with budget cuts frustrating Leslie's service initiatives. Leslie makes a deal with Chris and Ben to restore the Pawnee Harvest Festival, with the Parks Department being eliminated if the festival fails. After weeks of planning, the festival becomes a tremendous success. Chris returns from Indianapolis to become Pawnee's acting city manager, while Ben also takes a job in Pawnee. April and Andy start dating and marry in a surprise ceremony. Tom quits his city hall job to form Entertainment 720 with his friend Jean-Ralphio, which fails due to lavish spending, forcing Tom to return to the Parks Department. Leslie and Ben show romantic interest, though Chris has a rule preventing a superior from dating an employee. Despite this, they begin secretly dating. In the fourth season, Leslie campaigns for city council, realizing she must break up with Ben to avoid scandal. Ben and Leslie restart their relationship, and Ben sacrifices his job to save Leslie from losing hers due to Chris' workplace romance policy. The Parks Department volunteers as her campaign staff, with Ben as campaign manager. Leslie's campaign faces numerous setbacks against her opponent Bobby Newport and his campaign manager Jennifer Barkley. In the fifth season, Leslie becomes a City Councilor but faces opposition from locals and fellow councilmen. Ben works on a congressional campaign in Washington, DC, alongside April. Ron begins a romantic relationship with Diane. Ben returns to Pawnee and proposes to Leslie, and they get married midway through the season. Tom starts a successful business, Rent-A-Swag, that rents high-end clothing to teenagers. Leslie and Ben plan a fundraising event for the park, now called the Pawnee Commons, and have an impromptu wedding in City Hall. Later, Leslie's changes lead to locals petitioning for her recall. The sixth season begins with Eagleton being absorbed by Pawnee after declaring bankruptcy. As governments merge, Leslie loses the recall vote and returns to the Parks Department full-time, while Ben is voted in as the next City Manager. Tom sells Rent-A-Swag to Jean-Ralphio's father, Dr. Saperstein, in a cash settlement and opens a restaurant called "Tom's Bistro." Ann and Chris, now in a relationship and expecting a baby, leave Pawnee for Michigan. To gain public support for the merger, the Parks Department holds a Unity Concert. Leslie reveals she is pregnant with triplets and takes the job as Regional Director for the National Park Service in Chicago, immediately submitting a proposal to bring the job to Pawnee. The seventh season, which aired in 2015, takes place in 2017. Ron and Leslie are enemies because Ron's company tore down Ann's old house to build an apartment building. Ben convinces technology company Gryzzl to bring free Wi-Fi to Pawnee. Gryzzl engages in intense data mining, prompting Ron, whose construction company, Very Good Building and Development Company, is handling their projects, to reconnect with Leslie to correct the issue. Numerous actors made recurring guest appearances, including Pamela Reed as Leslie's mother and fellow politician Marlene Griggs-Knope, Ben Schwartz as Tom's friend Jean-Ralphio, Jenny Slate as Jean-Ralphio's twin sister Mona-Lisa, Jama Williamson as Tom's ex-wife Wendy, Mo Collins as morning talk show host Joan Callamezzo, Jay Jackson as broadcaster Perd Hapley, Alison Becker as reporter Shauna Malwae-Tweep, Darlene Hunt as activist Marcia Langman, and Andy Forrest as Andy's frequent shoeshine customer Kyle. Megan Mullally, the real-life wife of Nick Offerman, portrayed Ron's second ex-wife Tammy, while Patricia Clarkson played his first ex-wife, also named Tammy. Lucy Lawless and Jon Glaser had recurring roles: Lawless as Ron's love interest and later wife Diane Lewis, and Glaser as Leslie's archenemy on the city council, Jeremy Jamm. Mullally's performance was well received, making producers more comfortable using celebrity guest actors in later episodes. Other celebrity guests included Blake Anderson, Fred Armisen, Will Arnett, Kristen Bell, H. Jon Benjamin, Matt Besser, Chris Bosh, Louis C.K., The Decemberists, Sam Elliott, Will Forte, Ginuwine, Michael Gross, Jon Hamm, Nick Kroll, John Larroquette, Andrew Luck, Letters to Cleo, Natalie Morales, Parker Posey, Kathryn Hahn, Andy Samberg, J. K. Simmons, Roy Hibbert, Detlef Schrempf, Justin Theroux, Wilco, Henry Winkler, Peter Serafinowicz, and Yo La Tengo. Paul Rudd appeared in several season four episodes as Bobby Newport and returned for two episodes in the final season. The series featured cameos by real-life political figures such as then-Vice President Joe Biden, Senator Barbara Boxer, former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, Senator John McCain, First Lady Michelle Obama, former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, and Senators Olympia Snowe, Cory Booker, and Orrin Hatch. Immediately after Ben Silverman became co-chairman of NBC's entertainment division in 2007, he asked Greg Daniels to create a spin-off of The Office. Daniels co-created Parks and Recreation with Michael Schur, who had been a writer on The Office. The two spent months considering ideas, debating whether to make it a stand-alone or a spin-off, eventually abandoning the original spin-off plan because they "couldn't find the right fit." They considered a series about a local government official rebuilding a political career after a public humiliation, which later influenced Ben Wyatt's backstory. After Amy Poehler agreed to play the lead, they decided the series would focus on an optimistic bureaucrat in small-town government. Production was delayed to accommodate Poehler's pregnancy. The idea was inspired by the portrayal of local politics in The Wire and the renewed optimism about politics following the 2008 U.S. presidential election. The staff also wanted to build a show around a female relationship, specifically Leslie Knope and Ann Perkins. Reports that Daniels and Schur were developing a show together led to press speculation it would be a spin-off of The Office, but the producers insisted it would be entirely independent. Their concept shared elements with The Office, particularly the mockumentary format and encouragement of improvisation, even though episodes were scripted. The series was scheduled as a mid-season replacement and was rushed to meet its April 9, 2009, premiere date. Before settling on "Parks and Recreation," the name "Public Service" was considered but rejected by network officials who feared it would be seen as mocking the idea. Schur said they approached casting by seeking "the funniest people and we'll tailor the roles to them." Poehler left Saturday Night Live to star in Parks and Recreation as Leslie Knope. It was only after she was cast that Daniels and Schur established the series' general concept and wrote the pilot script. Rashida Jones was among the first cast members, having previously played Karen Filippelli on The Office. She departed in the middle of season six and returned for a guest appearance later in the season, returning in the series finale and the COVID-19 pandemic special. Paul Schneider was cast as Mark Brendanawicz and initially felt insecure about the role. He left after the second season, and the character is not referenced again. Similarly, Daniels and Schur had intended to cast Aziz Ansari from the earliest stages. While Aubrey Plaza was in Los Angeles, casting director Allison Jones, who had cast her in a film, asked her to attend a meeting with a showrunner developing a pilot. A fan of The Office, Plaza agreed. At the meeting, Daniels asked Plaza about life and death, and she pitched the idea of a smart, disinterested intern as a contrast to Poehler's character. The producers liked the concept and created April Ludgate. Chris Pratt was originally intended as a guest star with Andy Dwyer appearing only in the first season, but the producers liked him so much that they made him a regular starting in season two. Adam Scott left Party Down to join as Ben Wyatt, starting in the penultimate second-season episode, "The Master Plan." Nick Offerman had auditioned for Michael Scott in The Office, which went to Steve Carell, and was considered for another role but was cast as Ron Swanson because NBC felt he wouldn't fit a character who would later kiss Jones. Rob Lowe was introduced as Chris Traeger alongside Scott and was initially expected to leave after guest appearances, but later signed a multi-year contract to become a regular. He departed in the season six episode "Ann and Chris" and returned in the series finale and the 2020 special. Jim O'Heir and Retta made regular appearances as Garry "Jerry" Gergich and Donna Meagle from the first season, though their personalities were not fully developed until the second season. A throwaway joke in "Practice Date" established Jerry as the inept co-worker the department mocks. Donna was developed as a sassy hedonist with a mysterious life. They became regular cast members in the third season and were added to the opening credits in the sixth season. Billy Eichner was a recurring cast member as Craig Middlebrooks in season six and began being billed as a regular in the fourth episode of season seven. Deedle-Dee Productions and Universal Media Studios produced the series starting with the first season; Fremulon and 3 Arts Entertainment joined starting in the second season. The series was created by Greg Daniels and Michael Schur, who served as executive producers with Howard Klein, who previously worked with Daniels and Schur on The Office. Schur served as showrunner, with Amy Poehler and Morgan Sackett as producers. Dean Holland, an editor on The Office, also edited Parks and Recreation. Mike Scully, a former executive producer and showrunner for The Simpsons, joined as a consulting producer in the middle of the first season. Allison Jones, who worked as a casting director on The Office, served in the same role at the start of Parks and Recreation, along with Nancy Perkins, for whom the character Ann Perkins was named. Dorian Frankel became the casting director starting in the second season. Alan Yang, Harris Wittels, and Katie Dippold, all screenwriters for the series, also worked as executive story editors. The pilot episode was written by Daniels and Schur and directed by Daniels. Daniels also directed the second-season episode "Hunting Trip," while Schur made his directorial debut with the first-season finale "Rock Show" and wrote or directed several other episodes, including "Sister City," "The Master Plan," and "Time Capsule." Poehler wrote three episodes: "Telethon" in season 2, "The Fight" in season 3, and "The Debate" in season 4 (for which she was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series). She also co-wrote "Second Chance" in season 6, the series' 100th episode.

The pilot episode was written by Daniels and Schur and directed by Daniels. Schur made his directorial debut with the first-season finale "Rock Show," and wrote or directed several episodes including "Sister City," "The Master Plan," and "Time Capsule." Poehler wrote three episodes: "Telethon" in season 2, "The Fight" in season 3, and "The Debate" in season 4, for which she was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series; she also co-wrote "Second Chance," the series' 100th episode, and "One Last Ride," the series finale, with Schur. Poehler directed three episodes: "The Debate" in season 4, "Article Two" in season 5, and "Gryzzlbox" in season 7. Nick Offerman wrote "Lucky" in season 4 and directed season 5's "Correspondents' Lunch" and season 6's "Flu Season 2"; Adam Scott directed season 6's "Farmers Market." Dean Holland directed about thirty episodes of the series. Norm Hiscock, a consulting producer, wrote episodes including the first-season finale "Rock Show" and the second-season premiere "Pawnee Zoo." Other regular screenwriters included Katie Dippold, Dan Goor, Aisha Muharrar, Harris Wittels, and Alan Yang. Frequent directors include Dean Holland, Randall Einhorn, Troy Miller, and Jason Woliner, with others such as Jeffrey Blitz, Paul Feig, Tucker Gates, Seth Gordon, Nicole Holofcener, Beth McCarthy-Miller, Michael McCullers, and Charles McDougall guest-directing one or two episodes. The writers researched local California politics and attended Los Angeles City Council meetings; Schur noted that community hearings were often attended only by those opposed to proposals, which became a key element of town hall scenes and inspired the "Canvassing" episode. Scott Albright, a California city planner, provided direct feedback for the Mark Brendanawicz character, and the inspiration for Ron Swanson's anti-government views came from a real-life encounter Schur had with a libertarian official who said, "I don't really believe in the mission of my job." The concept of turning a construction pit into a park was used to bring characters together toward a common goal; the writers originally intended the pit to become a park only in the series finale, but changed plans and filled it in during the second-season episode "Kaboom." Daniels and Schur wrote the pilot script in mid-2008; early drafts portrayed Leslie and Mark as less likable, and changes were made based on focus group and press tour feedback, including Mark now backing Leslie due to admiration for her passion and drive, rather than supporting her plan for Ann Perkins. The writing staff avoided cynical humor and emphasized genuine character appreciation. The first-season episodes were developed quickly and treated as a single pilot. Audience feedback during the first season indicated Leslie Knope seemed unintelligent and "ditzy," prompting the writers to portray her as an overeager, capable woman starting in season two. Significant changes in season two included deepening the Leslie and Ron Swanson relationship, transforming Andy from a villain to a lovable man-child, and having Tom and April be intimidated by Leslie rather than scornful of her. The construction pit story arc was moved on from after "Kaboom," as early episodes had led viewers to believe the entire show revolved around filling the pit. Starting in the middle of season two, the writing staff drew inspiration from The Contender (2000), which features a female politician facing scrutiny in a male-dominated political arena, similar to Leslie's challenges. Financial difficulties in late season two and three reflected the 2008 global financial crisis. The introduction of Chris Traeger and Ben Wyatt as state auditors and the subsequent government shutdown were inspired by real-world news reports about state service shutdowns during the recession. A seven-episode harvest festival arc in season three helped unite the characters, similar to the construction pit, because the first six episodes were filmed early and needed a focused storyline to keep the writing staff organized. The romance between Leslie and Ben was inspired by The Remains of the Day, a story about repressed romantic feelings in a repressive social system, which Schur compared to modern government. Like The Office, Parks and Recreation used a single-camera, cinéma vérité style with no studio audience or laugh track, and characters were filmed by a documentary crew that was never seen or heard. The actors were encouraged to improvise, and many improvised lines made it into the final cut. Schur believed the mockumentary style was fitting for a government-focused show because it highlights differences between public and private behavior. The producers approached each episode as a real documentary, typically shooting 35–40 minutes and cutting it down to 22 minutes, discarding much extra footage; the original pilot cut was 48 minutes long. The team filmed about nine pages of script per day. The pilot used a technique inspired by The Five Obstructions, featuring intercut camera angles on the same person, and used jump cuts, such as in the scene where Leslie repeatedly seeks permission from Ron to pursue the pit project. Early in the season, editor Dean Holland developed a technique of intercutting improvised lines from Poehler's performance in "The Reporter" into a brief montage. Principal photography began on February 18, 2009, less than two months before the premiere, but was delayed because Poehler was pregnant when she signed on. Filming took place in Southern California; the Pawnee government building and hallway scenes were shot at Pasadena City Hall, while the parks and recreation department interiors and City Hall courtyard were filmed on a studio set with water systems simulating rain and fake pigeons. The set also included four hallways for Ann Perkins' hospital scenes. The construction pit was dug at an undeveloped property in Van Nuys, with residents' permission sought and the site guarded 24 hours a day. Outdoor scenes were filmed on location in Los Angeles, including public forum scenes in a middle school and a town meeting at the Toluca Lake Sports Center. Other Eagleton scenes were shot at the Huntington Library and Botanical Gardens in San Marino. The elaborate harvest festival and corn maze sets were filmed at Los Angeles Pierce College in Woodland Hills, and the aerial shot at the end of the episode was the most expensive shot in the series. Toward the end of season two, Poehler became pregnant again, forcing the production of season three to begin early and film six additional episodes to meet a projected September 2010 air date. NBC delayed the third season's premiere to the beginning of 2011 to run its new comedy Outsourced in a two-hour block, allowing all sixteen episodes to be filmed before airing. This gave the cast and crew additional time to re-edit or add new material, though it was frustrating for them. BMI was hired as music consultants to find a theme song; with less than three weeks until the premiere, composers were given five days to submit entries, with the winner receiving $7,500 for full rights. The winning song was written by Gaby Moreno and Vincent Jones. Schur said the theme song was chosen because it effectively established the show as set in a normal, everyday American town. The show does not use composed background music due to its realistic mockumentary style. Several songs were written for Andy Dwyer's band Mouse Rat; Pratt sings and plays guitar, Mark Rivers plays drums, Andrew Burlinson plays guitar, and Alan Yang plays bass. Rivers wrote most of the music performed by Mouse Rat. The band played live during filming. "The Pit" from "Rock Show" chronicles Andy's fall into the pit and broken legs; Pratt wrote "Ann," a ballad about Ann Perkins, featured in "Boys' Club"; Schur wrote the lyrics to "November," featured in "The Master Plan" about April Ludgate. In "Telethon," Andy performs "Sex Hair," about how to tell if someone has had sex by their hair being matted. In "Li'l Sebastian," Andy performs "5,000 Candles in the Wind," a tribute to Elton John's "Candle in the Wind" as requested by Leslie. The song was performed by the cast in the 2020 reunion special. A Mouse Rat album, The Awesome Album, was released on August 27, 2021, on vinyl, CD, cassette, and digital download by Dualtone Records and Entertainment 720 (a fictional company created by Tom Haverford). The album was announced with the release of two singles: "The Pit" from the season 1 finale and "Two Birds Holding Hands" from the season 3 episode "Andy and April's Fancy Party."

In the episode "Telethon," Andy performs the song "Sex Hair," which explains how one can tell if someone has had sex by examining their matted hair. In "Li'l Sebastian," Andy sings a tribute titled "5,000 Candles in the Wind," named because Leslie asks him to write a song like Elton John’s "Candle in the Wind" but 5,000 times better, and this song was performed by the show’s cast in the 2020 reunion special. A Mouse Rat album, The Awesome Album, was released on August 27, 2021, by Dualtone Records and Entertainment 720 (a fictional company created by Tom Haverford), available on vinyl, CD, cassette, and digital download. The album was announced with the release of two singles: "The Pit" from the season 1 finale "Rock Show" and "Two Birds Holding Hands" from the season 3 episode "Andy and April's Fancy Party." It features guest vocals from Nick Offerman as Ron Swanson and Jeff Tweedy as Scott Tanner. Pratt stated on Rob Lowe’s podcast Parks and Recollection that he was not involved in the project or its promotion. The album debuted at number 2 on Comedy Albums, number 11 on Heatseekers Albums, and number 17 on Top Album Sales on the weekly Billboard charts. Parks and Recreation aired in the United States on NBC at 8:30 pm Thursdays during its first two seasons as part of the Comedy Night Done Right line-up, moved to 9:30 pm during its third season as a mid-season replacement, returned to 8:30 pm in September 2011 for the fourth season, and moved back to 9:30 pm on Thursdays in 2012 for the fifth season. In Australia, it aired on Channel Seven’s digital channel 7mate; in Canada, it was simsubbed on City; in India, on Zee Café; in the Philippines, on Jack TV; in South Africa, on M-Net; and in the UK, it began airing on BBC Four in 2013 for the first three seasons before moving to Dave in summer 2015 starting with season 4. In March 2011, Universal Media Studios announced plans to sell the syndication rights, with Comedy Central, FX, and Spike as possible buyers. Syndicated episodes aired on NBCUniversal’s Esquire Network (after relaunching from Style) and WGN America. The pilot episode served as the first official broadcast of FXX when it launched on September 2, 2013, followed by an all-day marathon, marking the first time the show aired off-network. The series debuted on Comedy Central in the United States on January 21, 2019, with select episodes available to stream on their website and app, and Comedy Central holds the rights through 2024. In June 2020, the show also began airing on IFC in the United States, which they held until 2024. By 2018, Parks and Recreation was available on Hulu, Netflix, and Amazon Prime Video; viewership on Hulu increased by 32% in 2017, and according to Nielsen, it was one of the ten most-streamed shows on Netflix in 2018 based on time spent watching; Jumpshot analytics showed it had the third most views for 2018. In September 2019, it was announced the show would leave those streaming services for Peacock, NBCUniversal’s then-forthcoming streaming service, in October 2020; the streaming deal was reported to be worth nine figures. A limited number of rotating episodes were available through the Comedy Central app and website. In April 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, NBC aired a special episode centered on Leslie trying to stay connected with current and former residents of Pawnee during social distancing; the cast returned for the special, which benefited Feeding America’s COVID-19 response, and it aired on April 30, 2020. According to Schur, the special took about three weeks to complete; Morgan Sackett, who previously directed episodes, directed it, and original writers including Megan Amram, Dave King, Joe Mande, Aisha Muharrar, Matt Murray, and Jen Statsky created the script in three days; cast members were sent camera rigs and iPhones to record their parts, which took four days; visual effects from The Good Place (also created by Schur) were used to make the special look like the characters were not just sitting alone in their homes. Before the premiere, the first season received criticism; a March 18, 2009, leaked report to writer Nikki Finke showed focus groups responded poorly to a rough-cut pilot, calling it a "carbon copy" of The Office, describing it as predictable, slow-paced, and lacking in character development, with some noting a lack of strong male characters, particularly a "datable" lead; Schur insisted the pilot was re-edited at least four times after the focus groups; early feedback left many critics and industry observers skeptical. After airing, the first season received generally mixed reviews with a Metacritic score of 58 out of 100; critics noted the show was too similar to The Office and that Knope resembled Michael Scott; some found the tone too mean-spirited, and while individual cast members were praised, supporting characters were seen as underdeveloped; the season finale "Rock Show" received better reviews, with many declaring the show had finally found its tone and Leslie Knope’s character in particular. The 2009–10 season marked the most impressive comeback in broadcast comedy history, going from being dismissed as a flawed imitation of The Office to being named among the best shows of the year. Season two received better reviews with a Metacritic score of 71 out of 100, indicating "generally favorable reviews"; several publications named it among the best shows of 2009, including the Los Angeles Times, Chicago Tribune, Time, Entertainment Weekly, GQ, New York magazine, The Star-Ledger, San Francisco Chronicle, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Paste, IGN, and TV Squad; reviewers called it one of the most impressive comebacks in television history; some noted the supporting cast had better material and that Amy Poehler’s character had become less over-the-top and more human; others praised the removal of stale subplots like Leslie’s crush on Mark and the decision to fill in the pit, which freed the show for more stories and better scripts. Critical acclaim continued into the third season, which holds a Metacritic score of 83 out of 100, indicating "universal acclaim"; Steve Heisler of The A.V. Club said it became even better than in season two; Henry Hanks of CNN called it "a near-flawless season"; in TIME magazine’s 2012 year-end top 10 lists, Parks and Recreation was named the top TV series. The show appeared on the February 11, 2011, cover of Entertainment Weekly, which called it "the smartest comedy on TV" and included an article titled "101 Reasons to Love Parks and Recreation." Poehler said the first season struggled due to high expectations from comparisons to The Office, and hoped audiences would judge the show on its own; Schur believed early criticism stemmed from audiences not being familiar with the characters, and that viewers would enjoy them more upon better understanding. Poehler received wide praise for her performance from the beginning; reviewers even those who disliked the show said her talent, timing, and likability elevated the series. Offerman received strong praise for his minimalist and understated performance as Ron Swanson, considered a breakout character; Steve Heisler of GQ wrote that Ron Swanson was a major part of the show’s "creative resurgence"; by the end of season two, the character had a cult status; Jonah Weiner of Slate called Swanson "Parks and Recreation's secret weapon." Plaza’s portrayal of April received critical praise and was considered a breakout character; The New York Times said "all the characters were funny and well imagined, but Aubrey Plaza was particularly memorable as April"; Vanity Fair regarded April as "an avatar for millennial jadedness and skepticism"; The Daily Beast wrote Plaza was "one of the greatest elements" of the series, bringing both comedy and pathos. Reviewers consistently praised Aziz Ansari as Tom Haverford and Chris Pratt as Andy Dwyer; Jonah Weiner said the brightest spot in the first season was Ansari as Tom Haverford, who came "wickedly alive" as a faux player; Scott Meslow of The Atlantic said Ansari made Tom petulant, sexist, and materialistic without being unlikable; New York magazine writer Steve Kandell said Andy Dwyer usually steals episodes he appears in. In 2019, Parks and Recreation was ranked 54th on The Guardian’s list of the 100 best TV shows of the 21st century; Vox and Rolling Stone both named it the show that "defined" the cultural zeitgeist of the Obama Presidency. Alan Sepinwall wrote in Rolling Stone that few series have been as clearly tied to a moment—specifically a presidential administration—as Parks and Rec, noting the show’s belief in government’s power to improve lives and community responsibility, making it a standard-bearer for the hopefulness of the Obama era. National Review argued that even funny shows like Parks and Rec flatter those in power, with self-proclaimed nerds and wonks adopting Leslie Knope as a role model for believing government is a force for good. U.S. News & World Report commented on the series finale; James Poniewozik of Time argued that Parks became network TV’s best and brightest sitcom by embodying the idea that all politics is local, and that it promoted the idea that government must do things the private sector can’t or won’t, like preserving public spaces, aligning with a small-town, populist tradition seen in Friday Night Lights and It’s a Wonderful Life. Poehler stated she would love it if ratings went up and up, and that she felt the show had done a good job being inviting and friendly to new viewers, but otherwise was unsure what else could be done. Parks and Recreation struggled in the Nielsen ratings throughout its run; the premiere was seen by 6.88 million viewers, described as a strong opening comparable to 30 Rock; viewership declined weekly, ending the first season with a low of 4.29 million for the final episode and an average of 5.97 million, ranking 94th out of 193 network shows; low viewership challenged NBC, which trailed CBS, ABC, and Fox, and was affected by Jay Leno’s move to a 10:00 pm slot; at the end of the season, cast and crew were stressed about renewal. Despite low ratings, the show was renewed for a sixth season on May 9, 2013; NBC had a financial incentive because it owns distribution rights via NBCUniversal Television Distribution, and the sixth season passed the 100-episode milestone, making it more viable for syndication. In 2010, Amy Poehler was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her second season performance; Parks and Recreation was also nominated for the Television Critics Association Award for Outstanding Achievement in Comedy and Individual Achievement in Comedy for Nick Offerman in the second season; the second-season premiere episode, "Pawnee Zoo," won the GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Individual Episode.

Parks and Recreation received an overall average rating of 5.1 million viewers, ranking as the 116th highest-rated network series during the 2010–11 television season. Michael Schur partially attributed the consistently low viewership to a general decline in NBC's ratings and shifting viewer habits caused by the proliferation of available channels. Despite these low ratings, the series was renewed for a sixth season on May 9, 2013. NBC had a financial incentive to continue the show because it owns the distribution rights through NBCUniversal Television Distribution; the sixth season pushed the series past the 100-episode milestone, enhancing its potential for syndication. In 2010, Amy Poehler was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her performance in the second season, and Parks and Recreation was nominated for the Television Critics Association Award for Outstanding Achievement in Comedy and Individual Achievement in Comedy for Nick Offerman in the same season. The second-season premiere episode, "Pawnee Zoo," won the GLAAD Media Award for Outstanding Individual Episode (in a Series without a Regular LGBT Character). The series also received two nominations from Entertainment Weekly's EWwy Awards in 2010: Best Comedy Series and Best Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series for Offerman. In 2011, Parks and Recreation was nominated for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series, and Amy Poehler earned her second Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series. In June 2011, the show was nominated for three awards at the inaugural Critics' Choice Television Awards: Best Comedy Series, Best Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for Poehler, and Best Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series for Offerman. That same month, it received four TCA Awards: Program of the Year, Outstanding Achievement in Comedy, and Individual Achievement in Comedy for Offerman and Poehler, with Offerman hosting the TCA Awards ceremony. In 2012, the series won a Peabody Award. In January 2014, Poehler won her first Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Television Series Comedy. The first season of Parks and Recreation was released on DVD in region 1 on September 8, 2009, including all six episodes, an "Extended Producer's Cut" of the season finale "Rock Show," cast and crew commentary tracks for each episode, and about 30 minutes of deleted scenes. The second season was released in a four-disc region 1 set on November 30, 2010, featuring extended episodes for "The Master Plan" and "Freddy Spaghetti," two-and-a-half hours of deleted scenes, a third season preview, additional video clips, and audio commentaries for "Sister City," "Ron and Tammy," "Hunting Trip," "Woman of the Year," "The Master Plan," and "Freddy Spaghetti." The complete series Blu-ray was released by Universal Pictures Home Entertainment on June 15, 2021. In March 2019, during the tenth anniversary reunion at PaleyFest, the cast confirmed they would return for a revival if series creator Michael Schur developed an original, new idea; Schur stated, "I would never ever say never. The chance to do it again, should it arise, would be incredible, but we would only do it if we all felt like there was something compelling us to do it. If one single person said no, we wouldn't do it." In April 2020, the cast reprised their roles for a special episode created during the COVID-19 pandemic, which first aired on NBC and raised funds for Feeding America.
